title: Page Site / “Lost City” (15LO1)
summary: In Logan County, the Page Site is a Mississippian complex of at least 67 mounds, called by far the most extensive mound complex in Kentucky.
bodyMarkdown:
In Logan County lies the Page Site, recorded by archaeologists as 15LO1, a Mississippian mound complex. In the [Kentucky Heritage Council's survey of the Mississippi period](https://archaeology.ky.gov/Learn-More/Documents/Mississippi%20Period%20Chapter%20The%20Archaeology%20of%20Kentucky%20An%20update%20Volume%202.pdf), archaeologist David Pollack calls it "by far the most extensive mound complex in Kentucky." It is one of the clearest records of the farming towns that Native people built in south-central Kentucky about a thousand years ago.

## Mounds and the people buried there

William S. Webb and William D. Funkhouser of the University of Kentucky investigated the site in the late 1920s and published their findings in 1930. According to the Kentucky Heritage Council chapter, they counted at least 67 recognizable mounds. They excavated 18 of them, and most turned out to be mortuary mounds holding stone-lined cist graves.

These were the graves of the community's own dead, placed with care by their families. Modern archaeology treats such places as burial grounds that deserve respect, not as curiosities. The site's address is restricted on the [National Register of Historic Places record](https://npgallery.nps.gov/AssetDetail/NRIS/85002819), which helps protect it.

One mound stood apart. Mound 3 held no burials and may have been a platform mound, built in at least two stages. Webb and Funkhouser recovered about 300 pottery sherds from it, all tempered with crushed limestone.

## How old is it?

Dating the Page Site is not simple. The Heritage Council chapter describes a "Page phase" dated to roughly A.D. 900–1100. An earlier researcher, Allen, tentatively placed the site in the early Mississippi period, but the chapter notes that its age cannot be estimated precisely. The National Register file gives a broader period of significance, from 1000 to 1599.

What is clear is that the site belongs to the wider world of the [Mississippian culture](https://grokipedia.com/page/Mississippian_culture). Across the Southeast and Midwest, Mississippian communities grew maize, built earthen platform mounds and plazas, and buried their dead in mounds and cemeteries. The Page Site's limestone-tempered pottery and cist graves give it a regional character of its own.

## From burial ground to tourist stop

In the 1930s the site was developed as a heritage tourism attraction called "Lost City," according to the list of [National Register sites in Logan County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Register_of_Historic_Places_listings_in_Logan_County,_Kentucky). Like many attractions of that era, it presented Native graves and mounds as a mystery rather than as the home of known ancestors. Kentucky archaeologists today describe the site in terms of the people who lived and farmed there.

The site was listed on the National Register of Historic Places on November 14, 1985. The record lists it as privately owned.

## Kentucky today

The Page Site remains private land and is not open as a public park. Visitors who want to see a Mississippian town in Kentucky can go to [Wickliffe Mounds](/stories/wickliffe-mounds-mississippian-village-ballard-county/) in Ballard County. Other Mississippian sites in this collection include the [Tolu Site](/stories/tolu-site-mississippian-mounds-on-the-lower-ohio/) and [Jonathan Creek](/stories/jonathan-creek-mississippian-center/).
